inputs.original_text: The Punjab and Haryana High Court has granted regular bail to a man accused under national-security provisions and the Official Secrets Act, saying suspicion alone—of sharing sensitive information with someone in Pakistan—can’t justify keeping him locked up indefinitely. The alleged contact was with Karachi-based “Punjabi Kuri.” This looks less like a clear security case than a system using national-security labels to create a frightening story, then quietly stepping back when the evidence can’t support prolonged detention. Bail isn’t proof of innocence, but the accusations aren’t proof of guilt either.
inputs.modified_text: They wrapped this man in national-security charges over alleged contact with Karachi-based “Punjabi Kuri,” then the Punjab and Haryana High Court said suspicion alone couldn’t justify holding him indefinitely. That looks like the familiar play: use secrecy laws to manufacture fear and make an accusation sound like proof, then retreat once the case can’t sustain the detention. The bail doesn’t settle guilt or innocence—but the timing raises questions about who benefits from keeping the public frightened while the evidence remains uncertain.
